text: Most dinosaurs had small brains for their size, and probably were not very clever by human standards. But "dinosaur" covers thousands of kinds of animal over more than 160 million years. Big plant-eaters like Stegosaurus had tiny brains. Some small meat-eaters, like Troodon, had brains as big for their bodies as some living birds.
And some dinosaurs are clever by any standard. [[@crow-smart|Crows]] and parrots are dinosaurs, and they can use tools, remember faces and solve puzzles.

st.prompt: Scientists can't find fossil brains. How do they study dinosaur brains?

options.t: They scan the empty space inside the skull where the brain sat
They look at frozen dinosaur brains from Antarctica

st.reveal: The brain leaves its shape on the inside of the skull. A CT scanner, a kind of X-ray machine, maps that hollow space in 3D. The result is a model of the brain's size and shape, though not of how well it worked.

sec.t:
Brains are soft and rot quickly, so they almost never fossilise. Instead, scientists study the hollow inside the skull. In many dinosaurs the brain did not fill the space completely, so this gives an upper limit on brain size.

In the past, scientists poured liquid rubber into a skull to make a cast. Today they use CT scanners, a kind of [[@x-rays|X-ray]] machine, to map the space without harming the [[fossil|fossil]]. The scan shows which parts were large. Big smelling areas, called olfactory bulbs, mean a keen nose. Big areas at the back can mean sharp eyesight or good balance.

Troodon, a slim hunter from North America, had large eyes and one of the biggest brains for its body size of any non-bird dinosaur. In 1982, a Canadian scientist called Dale Russell playfully asked what Troodon might have become if it had kept [[evolve|evolving]]. He made a model of a big-headed, upright "dinosauroid". It was a thought experiment, not a real animal.

Scans show that brains grew larger, for their bodies, in the feathered dinosaurs closest to birds. Some had brains as big as early birds like Archaeopteryx, with large areas for sight and balance. So the "bird brain" was partly built before birds took to the air.

[[@trex-bite|T. rex]] had a big brain for a [[reptile|reptile]], and its smelling areas were very large. It probably had a strong sense of [[@nose-smell|smell]], good for finding prey or bodies from far away.

In 2023, a scientist estimated the number of nerve cells in T. rex's brain. She suggested it had about as many as a baboon, and might have been as smart as a monkey. Many other experts disagreed. In 2024, a larger team argued that T. rex's brain did not fill its skull, and that its nerve cell count was probably closer to a crocodile's.

That argument shows how hard the question is. Even in living animals, brain size is a rough guide. A crow's brain is tiny, yet its nerve cells are packed tightly, much more than in a [[mammal|mammal]] brain of the same size. Your [[@brain-works|own brain]] is clever because of how its parts connect, as well as how big it is. For dinosaurs we have the box, but not what was inside it.

text: The Hubble Space Telescope has helped show us how big, old and busy the universe is. It has photographed [[galaxy|galaxies]] so far away that their light left them more than 13 billion years ago. It helped measure the age of the universe at about 13.8 billion years. And it helped show that the universe is growing faster and faster.
Hubble was launched in 1990 by NASA, working with the European Space Agency. It is still working more than 35 years later, which makes it one of the most successful science instruments ever built.

st.reveal: Earth's air is always moving, which makes stars twinkle and pictures blur. It also blocks some kinds of light, like ultraviolet. From orbit, Hubble sees a steady, sharp sky.

sec.t:
Soon after launch, scientists realised something was badly wrong. Hubble's pictures were fuzzy. Its main mirror had been ground to slightly the wrong shape. The error was about 2 micrometres at the edges, around one-fiftieth the width of a human hair, but it was enough to spoil the focus.

The fix was a bit like giving Hubble [[@lenses-glasses|glasses]]. In December 1993, astronauts on the Space Shuttle Endeavour caught the telescope, installed a new camera and a set of small corrective mirrors, and released it again. The first sharp pictures were a huge relief. Astronauts returned four more times, the last in 2009, to fix parts and add better instruments.

In December 1995, [[astronomer|astronomers]] pointed Hubble at a tiny, empty-looking patch of sky, about as big as a tennis ball seen from 100 m away. They collected light for ten days.

The result, the Hubble Deep Field, showed about 3,000 [[@galaxies|galaxies]] in that speck alone. Each contains billions of stars. Later deep fields found even more. Since the sky is full of patches like that, astronomers now estimate there are hundreds of billions of galaxies in the part of the universe we can see.

Hubble helped show that almost every big galaxy has a giant [[@black-holes|black hole]] at its centre, millions or billions of times heavier than the Sun.

In 1998, two teams studying exploding stars in distant galaxies found that the universe's growth is [[@mystery-dark-energy|speeding up]]. Hubble's measurements were part of the evidence. The leaders of those teams won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2011, and the mysterious push behind it is called dark energy.

In July 1994, Hubble watched pieces of a broken [[comet|comet]] named [[@comets-famous|Shoemaker-Levy 9]] slam into [[@jupiter-giant|Jupiter]], leaving dark scars bigger than Earth in the planet's clouds.

Hubble's [[orbit|orbit]] is slowly sinking as thin traces of air drag on it. NASA expects it to keep working into the 2030s. The [[@webb-telescope|James Webb Space Telescope]], launched in 2021, has a bigger mirror and sees mainly [[infrared|infrared]] light. The two often look at the same objects and compare notes. Webb sees farther back in time. Hubble sees more of the visible and ultraviolet colours that Webb can't.

text: The far side of the Moon is the half that always faces away from Earth. It gets just as much sunshine as the near side, but nobody on Earth had seen it until a space probe flew behind the Moon in 1959.

It turned out to look very different. The side we see has large dark patches, called maria, Latin for "seas". These are old [[lava|lava]] plains. The far side has hardly any. Instead it is covered in [[crater|craters]] on top of craters, including the South Pole–Aitken basin, about 2,500 km across and one of the biggest impact basins in the Solar System.

st.reveal: The Moon turns once on its axis in the same time it takes to go once around Earth, about 27 days. So the same face always points towards us. Scientists call this tidal locking.

sec.h: Why we only see one face
sec.t:
The Moon does spin, but slowly. It turns once on its [[axis|axis]] in about 27 days, the same time it takes to go once around Earth. So the same face always points towards us, just as a dancer circling a partner keeps looking at them.

This didn't happen by chance. Long ago the Moon spun faster. Earth's [[gravity|gravity]] stretched it slightly into an egg shape, the same kind of pull that raises [[@tides|tides]] in our oceans. Earth's tug on that bulge slowly braked the Moon's spin until the two matched. Because the Moon wobbles a little in its [[orbit|orbit]], we actually get to see about 59% of its surface over time. The other 41% stays hidden.

Scientists think the answer lies in the crust, the Moon's outer rocky layer. On the far side it is much thicker. When giant space rocks hit the near side billions of years ago, melted rock from deep inside could push through the thin crust and flood the craters, making dark maria. On the far side, the thick crust mostly kept the lava down.

Why the crust is thicker there is still being studied. One idea is that heat from the young, glowing Earth kept the near side warmer for longer while the Moon cooled. The [[@moon-formed|Moon's own birth]], probably from a giant crash between Earth and another world, may also have played a part.

Landing on the far side is hard because there is no direct radio link to Earth. In 2018, China placed a relay satellite called Queqiao beyond the Moon to pass messages back and forth. In January 2019, its Chang'e 4 lander touched down in Von Kármán crater, the first landing on the far side. Its little [[rover|rover]], Yutu-2, kept exploring for years.

In June 2024, Chang'e 6 brought about 2 kg of far-side rock and soil back to Earth, the first ever. Scientists are studying them to learn when the far side's few lava flows happened. India's [[@chandrayaan|Chandrayaan]]-2 orbiter, circling since 2019, has mapped both sides from above.

[[astronomer|Astronomers]] have another dream for the far side. Because the Moon blocks the noise of radios, phones and TV from Earth, it could be the quietest place nearby to build a radio telescope and listen to the early universe.

text: Probably, yes. In 2013, the Hubble Space Telescope measured the colour of a planet called HD 189733b and found it was a deep cobalt blue, a bit like Earth seen from space. But the blue doesn't come from oceans. [[astronomer|Astronomers]] think it comes from tiny bits of silicate, the stuff glass is made from, floating in its clouds.

The planet is a giant, bigger than Jupiter, and it circles its star so closely that one year lasts just over two days. Its air is around 1,000 °C. If those glass particles fall as rain, they would be whipped sideways by winds estimated at about 7,000 km/h, about eight times faster than a passenger jet.

The planet's gravity pulls sideways

st.reveal: The planet is very close to its star and heated on one side. Hot gas rushes around it at an estimated 7,000 km/h or so. Anything falling from the clouds would be swept along, so the "rain" would race sideways.

Rain just means liquid or solid drops falling from clouds. On Earth it is water, but on other worlds it may be methane, sulphuric acid, iron or even glass, depending on how hot or cold the planet is.

sec.h: How do we know, from 64 light-years?
sec.t:
Nobody has seen the rain. Astronomers study planets like this when they pass in front of their star. Some starlight shines through the planet's thin outer air on the way to us, and different chemicals block different colours. By reading what is missing, scientists can guess what the air is made of, a method explained more in the story of [[@exoplanets|exoplanets]].

That's why the glass rain is an educated guess, not a photograph. In 2024, the James Webb Space Telescope found hydrogen sulphide on the same planet, the gas that makes rotten eggs smell. So this blue world might also stink.

sec.h: Weird rain in our own solar system
sec.t:
On Venus, clouds of sulphuric [[acid|acid]] drop acid rain. But the planet's surface is around 465 °C, so the drops evaporate long before landing. Rain that never reaches the ground has a name on Earth too: virga, those grey streaks you sometimes see hanging under clouds.

Saturn's moon [[@titan|Titan]] is colder than any freezer, about −180 °C. There, methane and ethane, which are gases on Earth, fall as rain. The drops are thought to be bigger than Earth raindrops and fall slowly, drifting down like snowflakes because Titan's [[gravity|gravity]] is weak and its air is thick. The rain fills real lakes and rivers.

Earth's rain is water because our planet sits at just the right temperature for water to be a gas, a liquid and a solid. Move Earth much closer to the Sun and the oceans would boil. Move it farther away and they would freeze.

Every planet has its own "rain" that matches its temperature. Super-hot worlds rain rock and metal. Freezing worlds rain chemicals we use as fuel. On ours, it is the plain water cycle that fills wells and rivers, described in the story of [[@clouds-rain|clouds and rain]]. And astronomers say that HD 189733b's rotten-egg air is one of the strangest [[@space-weird-smell|smells in space]] ever detected.

text: Dolphins talk with sound, because [[@sound-travel|sound travels]] far and fast underwater while light does not. They make two main kinds. Whistles help them keep in touch with their family and friends. Rapid clicks help them [[echolocation|echolocate]], which means finding things by listening to echoes.

The best-studied kind, the bottlenose dolphin, does something special with whistles. Each one invents its own signature whistle when it is a baby, and keeps it for life. Other dolphins learn it and copy it to call that dolphin, a bit like saying its name.
Nobody has found a dolphin grammar yet, so we can't call it a language. But it is far more than random noise.

quiz.reveal: A sleeping dolphin rests one half of its brain while the other half stays alert, often with one eye open. That way it can keep surfacing to breathe and watch for danger.

sec.t:
In 2013, two scientists in Scotland, Stephanie King and Vincent Janik, tested wild bottlenose dolphins. They recorded each dolphin's signature whistle, then played copies back through an underwater speaker. Dolphins answered when they heard their own whistle, and mostly ignored others.

Another study found that dolphins remember the whistles of old tank mates even after 20 years apart. That is longer than any other animal's social [[@memory|memory]] measured so far, apart from ours.

In Sarasota Bay in Florida, scientists have followed the same wild dolphin families since 1970. They have found that mothers whistle their own signature much more often when they have a new calf, perhaps helping the baby learn whose call to follow.

Dolphins use sound to work together, too. In the town of Laguna in southern Brazil, wild dolphins herd fish towards people standing in the shallows. Then the dolphins make a sudden dive or head slap, and the fishers throw their nets. Scientists say this partnership has gone on for well over a century, passed down through dolphin and human families alike.

The Ganges river dolphin lives in the muddy waters of the Ganga and Brahmaputra and their branches, flowing down from the [[@rivers-himalaya|Himalayan rivers]]. In murky water, good eyes are useless, and its eyes have no lens at all. It can sense light, but it finds food and its way almost entirely by clicking.

People along the river call it *susu*, after the sound it makes when it surfaces to breathe. It often swims tilted on its side, sweeping its long beak through the mud for fish and shrimps.

India made it the National Aquatic Animal in 2009. The first count along the country's rivers, published in 2025, found about 6,300 river dolphins.

Dolphins depend on [[@ears-hear|hearing]], so noise is a real problem for them. Ship engines, dams and dredging fill the water with sound that can drown out their calls. River dolphins also get tangled in fishing nets, and dams cut their rivers into pieces.

Some places are fighting back. The Vikramshila [[sanctuary|sanctuary]] in Bihar protects a stretch of the Ganga for river dolphins. At Chilika Lake in Odisha, boat tours watch another kind, the Irrawaddy dolphin. Like all dolphins, they are [[@whales-walked|whales']] close cousins, and their ancestors once walked on land.

text: Cuttlefish are soft-bodied sea animals, cousins of the octopus and squid. They are among the best colour-changers on Earth. When hunting, some cuttlefish make bands of dark colour ripple across their bodies, a display scientists call "passing cloud". Prey such as crabs and shrimps often stay still while it happens, which is why people say cuttlefish "hypnotise" them.

Nobody is sure exactly how it works. The rippling may confuse the prey's eyes, make it hard to judge the cuttlefish's distance, or simply look like moving shadows on the seabed. Once close enough, the cuttlefish shoots out two long [[tentacle|tentacles]] faster than you can blink and grabs its meal.

sec.t:
A cuttlefish's skin is packed with millions of tiny colour sacs called chromatophores. Each one holds yellow, red, brown or black [[pigment|pigment]], wrapped in a ring of muscle. When nerves tell the muscles to pull, the sac stretches open like a balloon and the colour spreads. When they relax, it shrinks to a dot.

Beneath those sacs are cells that reflect light, making shimmering blues and greens, and white patches. By controlling all these layers at once, a cuttlefish can change colour, pattern and even skin texture in under a second. It can raise little bumps to look like seaweed or coral. That is faster and more varied than a [[@power-chameleon|chameleon]].

Here is the puzzle. Cuttlefish eyes have W-shaped pupils and only one type of light [[sensor|sensor]], which suggests they cannot see colour as we do. Yet they match coloured backgrounds very well.

Scientists are still working out how. Their eyes can sense polarised light, a pattern in light waves that we can't see. Their skin may even contain light-sensitive [[protein|proteins]]. The W-shaped pupils may also help them pick up tiny differences in colour by blurring them slightly.

sec.h: Three hearts and a hidden shell
sec.t:
Like an [[@octopus-smart|octopus]], a cuttlefish has three hearts. Two pump blood through the gills and one pumps it around the body. Its blood is blue-green, because it uses copper to carry oxygen instead of iron.

Inside its back is a cuttlebone, a light, chalky shell full of tiny gas-filled chambers. By changing the amount of gas and liquid inside, the cuttlefish floats higher or sinks lower. Washed-up cuttlebones are sold in pet shops for birds to peck for calcium. Most cuttlefish live only a year or two. Common cuttlefish females lay clusters of eggs darkened with ink, which hang from seaweed like bunches of black grapes.

In 2021, scientists in Cambridge, England, tested cuttlefish with a version of the marshmallow test. Many waited for their favourite food, live shrimp, instead of eating crab right away. Some waited more than two minutes. The ones that waited longest were also the fastest learners in other tests.

Cuttlefish also squirt [[@octopus-ink|ink]] to escape. And the strangest part? Their brown ink was once used by artists and writers, and gave its name to a colour, sepia, as the story of [[@art-materials|old art materials]] shows.

text: The biggest machine people have ever built is the Large Hadron Collider, or LHC, a scientific instrument in a 27 km ring under France and Switzerland. The heaviest machine that can move on land is a German coal digger called Bagger 293. It weighs about 14,200 tonnes, roughly as much as 2,000 elephants.

Other giants include the longest ship ever made, the heaviest aeroplane and the slow, mighty vehicles that carry rockets to their launch pads. Each one was built because a job was simply too big for anything smaller.

sec.t:
Bagger 293 is a bucket-wheel excavator. That means it has a giant spinning wheel at the front with 20 buckets around its edge, each big enough to hold a small car. The wheel is more than 21 m across, as tall as a seven-storey building.

The whole machine is about 96 m tall and 225 m long, longer than two football fields. It works in open-pit coal mines in Germany, scraping away earth and coal. In one day it can move about 2,40,000 cubic metres of material. That would fill nearly 100 Olympic swimming pools. Yet it needs only a handful of workers to run it.

It moves on caterpillar tracks at well under 1 km/h. A snail would lose the race, but not by much.

The longest ship ever built was an oil tanker named Seawise Giant, later called Knock Nevis. It was about 458 m long, longer than the Empire State Building is tall. Fully loaded, it was too big to pass through the [[@suez-canal|Suez Canal]] or the English Channel. It was taken apart for scrap in 2010, at Alang in Gujarat, one of the world's biggest shipbreaking yards.

Today's biggest ships include giant container ships about 400 m long, carrying more than 20,000 containers each. Stacked end to end, those boxes would stretch more than 120 km.

The Antonov An-225 Mriya, from Ukraine, was the heaviest aeroplane ever built. It had six engines and a wingspan of about 88 m. It could take off weighing about 640 tonnes, and it once carried a single piece of cargo weighing nearly 190 tonnes.

Only one was ever completed. It was destroyed in 2022 at an airfield near Kyiv during the war in Ukraine.

NASA's two crawler-transporters were built in the 1960s to carry Saturn V moon rockets. Each weighs about 2,700 tonnes and is about the size of a baseball diamond. They still work today, carrying NASA's newest rockets to the launch pad in Florida.

With a rocket on top, a crawler moves at about 1.6 km/h. The ride to the pad takes hours. Its tracks are made of steel shoes, each weighing about a tonne.

India builds giants too. Indian Railways' WAG-12B electric locomotives, made at Madhepura in Bihar, are among the most powerful freight engines in the world, at 12,000 horsepower. Each can haul a train of about 6,000 tonnes.

Some of the most surprising giant machines work out of sight, deep underground, chewing through mountains to make the world's [[@extreme-longest-tunnels|longest tunnels]].

text: Paper is made from [[cellulose|cellulose]], the tough substance in plant cell walls. Most paper today starts as wood from trees, but it can also come from cotton, bamboo, straw, sugarcane waste or old paper.

First, the plant material is broken down into separate fibres. Wood is chopped into chips and then either ground up or cooked with chemicals until the fibres come apart. The fibres are mixed with lots of water to make a runny pulp. This is sprayed onto a fast-moving mesh belt. Water drains away through the holes, leaving a thin wet mat of tangled fibres. Rollers squeeze out more water, and heated drums dry the sheet. Finally, it is pressed smooth and wound onto giant rolls.
A modern paper machine can be longer than a football field and roll out paper faster than a car drives in a city.

st.prompt: Papermakers spread wet pulp on a fine screen. What holds the fibres together once the sheet dries?

options.t: The fibres themselves cling together as they dry
Glue is sprayed on top
Tiny staples

st.reveal: Plant fibres are made of cellulose, and as water dries out between them, the fibres form many small bonds with each other where they touch. Thousands of crossing fibres make a strong sheet. That's also why paper falls apart when it gets very wet.

d.try: Make your own paper. Tear old newspaper into small pieces and soak them in a bowl of water overnight. Squeeze and mash them with your hands into a soupy pulp. Dip an old net or a fine kitchen sieve into the pulp to collect a thin, even layer. Press it gently with a sponge to squeeze out water, then let it dry for a day or two and peel it off.
myth: Papyrus was the first paper.

Papyrus was made by laying thin strips of the papyrus plant's stem in a criss-cross pattern and pressing them together. True paper is made by breaking plant material down into separate fibres and forming them into a new sheet, an invention from China.

sec.t:
Look at the torn edge of a piece of paper with a magnifying glass, and you'll see fuzzy fibres sticking out. Each one is a tiny tube from a plant. When the pulp dries, these fibres press close together and form countless small bonds where they touch. Nothing else is needed to hold them.

Papermakers often add other things, such as clay to make the paper whiter and smoother, or a coating called sizing that stops ink from spreading. Without sizing, writing in ink on paper would look like writing on tissue.

Before paper, people in India often wrote on palm leaves and birch bark. Paper became more common from around the 1200s onward, and many towns developed their own paper-making workshops.

At Sanganer, near [[@jaipur|Jaipur]], families still make handmade paper using cotton rags, flowers and leaves, pressed and dried in the sun. The Kumarappa National Handmade Paper Institute in Jaipur teaches these skills. Handmade paper is often used for wedding cards, notebooks and art.

Bamboo is also used to make paper in India, because it grows very quickly and has long, strong fibres. Paper factories in places like Assam and Odisha have used it for decades.

Paper is one of the easiest materials to recycle. Old paper is soaked in water, stirred into pulp, cleaned of ink and staples, then made into new sheets. Each time, though, the fibres get shorter and weaker. After about five to seven rounds, they are too short to bind and are often turned into egg cartons or [[@newspapers|newspapers]].

Recycling paper saves trees, water and energy. A tonne of recycled paper can replace the wood from many trees, and the factories make less pollution. From a crumpled school worksheet to a cereal box, much of what you [[@recycling|recycle]] can become paper again.

text: Simple traffic lights run on a timer. A controller box beside the road switches them in a fixed pattern: green for a set time, then [[amber|amber]], then red, and round again.

Many lights are smarter. They use [[sensor|sensors]] to find out where cars are waiting. The most common sensor is a loop of wire buried in the road just before the stop line. Electricity flowing through it makes a magnetic field. When a car stops on top, its metal changes the field, and the controller knows someone is there. Other lights use [[@cameras-how|cameras]] or radar mounted on poles. Pedestrians can push a button to ask for their turn.
The controller is a small computer. It follows a set of rules, an [[@algorithms|algorithm]], to decide which road gets green next and for how long.

st.prompt: In many places, a coil of wire is buried in the road just before the stop line. What does it do?

options.t: It senses the metal of a car stopped above it
It heats the road to melt snow
It weighs each car

st.reveal: Electricity runs through the coil, making a magnetic field. When a large metal object like a car sits above it, the field changes, and the controller knows a vehicle is waiting. You can sometimes spot the loop as a rectangle cut into the road surface.

First, change the lights every 20 seconds, no matter what. Then try changing them only when a "car" is waiting. Which way keeps your cars moving better?
myth: Pressing the crossing button again and again makes the light change faster.

One press is enough to tell the controller someone wants to cross. Extra presses usually do nothing. In some busy cities, many buttons are switched off at certain times of day, because the lights run on a fixed timer anyway.

wire loops in the road, cameras and radar

sec.t:
The first traffic signal was put up in December 1868 outside the Houses of Parliament in [[@london|London]]. It was designed by a railway engineer, John Peake Knight, and copied railway signals. By day, a policeman raised arms on a pole. At night, he turned a lamp lit by gas to show red or green.

A few weeks later, a gas leak made the lamp explode, injuring the policeman. The idea was dropped for decades. Traffic lights returned in the USA once electric lamps were common. In 1914, the city of Cleveland, Ohio, put up electric red and green lights, and in 1920 a Detroit policeman named William Potts added a third colour.

Red is almost always at the top of a vertical traffic light, or on the left or right in a horizontal one, depending on the country. This helps people who are colour-blind, who may find red and green hard to tell apart. They can read the signal by which lamp is lit.

Red probably means stop because railways used it for danger first, and red is the colour many cultures already linked with warning. In India, many signals add a countdown timer showing how many seconds are left. Drivers can switch off their engines at long reds, saving fuel and cutting fumes.

sec.h: Lights that talk to each other
sec.t:
On a long main road, engineers can time a chain of lights so a driver going at the right speed meets green after green. This is called a green wave. Some cities, including [[@los-angeles|Los Angeles]], link thousands of signals to a control centre. [[@how-traffic-cameras|Cameras watch the traffic]], and computers adjust the timings minute by minute.

Ambulances and fire engines in some cities can turn lights green ahead of them. In the future, cars may talk directly to traffic lights by radio, and [[@self-driving|self-driving cars]] will need to read signals as reliably as any human driver.

text: Theatre, acting out stories in front of an audience, began in many places. Two of the oldest traditions we know well are from ancient Greece and ancient India.

In Athens, more than 2,500 years ago, plays grew out of religious festivals for the god Dionysus, with songs, dance and [[@art-masks-world|masked actors]]. In India, [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] drama was described in a great guide called the *Natyashastra*, roughly 2,000 years old, which explains acting, music, dance, costume and stage design. Theatre also grew separately in China, Japan, Southeast Asia and elsewhere, often from festivals, storytelling and dance. Nobody can point to a single first play.

st.prompt: In ancient Greek theatre, why did actors wear large masks?

options.t: So one actor could play several characters and faces could be seen from far away
To keep warm in winter
Because acting was against the law without one

st.reveal: Greek plays often had only three main actors, so each played several roles by changing masks. The big, clear expressions could be read from distant seats, and some think the mask's shape helped carry the voice.

d.try: Make two simple masks from paper plates, one happy and one angry. With a friend, act out a short scene where you swap masks halfway through without saying anything. Can the audience follow the change in mood just from the masks and your body?
myth: Theatre began in one place and spread from there to the rest of the world.
Theatre grew up in many places, including Greece, India, China and Japan, often from religious festivals, storytelling and dance. These traditions developed in different ways, mostly on their own.

sec.t:
Every spring, Athens held a big festival for Dionysus, god of wine and celebration. At first, a chorus of men sang and danced stories together. Greek tradition says that in the 500s BCE a performer named Thespis stepped out from the chorus and spoke as a character. That's why actors are sometimes called thespians.

Soon writers like Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides were writing tragedies about gods, kings and terrible choices. Others wrote comedies that made fun of politicians. Plays were performed as a competition, and [[@ancient-greece|ancient Greek]] citizens took them very seriously.

sec.h: The theatre that carries a whisper

sec.t:
The *Natyashastra* is said to have been written by a sage named Bharata. Scholars date it anywhere from about 200 BCE to 200 CE. It is a huge handbook covering how to move the eyes, hands and feet, how to build a stage and how to stir the audience's feelings.

Its most famous idea is *rasa*, the emotional flavour a performance creates, such as love, courage, sorrow or wonder. A good play, it says, leaves the audience tasting these feelings, the way a good meal leaves many flavours. Indian classical dances, including [[@kathak|Kathak]] and [[@bharatanatyam|Bharatanatyam]], still use ideas from it.

The poet [[@kalidasa|Kalidasa]], who probably lived around the 4th or 5th century CE, wrote some of the most loved Sanskrit plays. The best known, *Abhijnanashakuntalam*, tells of the king Dushyanta and Shakuntala, who forget and find each other again. When it was translated into English in 1789, it caused a stir among European writers.

In Kerala, Kutiyattam keeps a form of [[@indian-theatre|Sanskrit theatre]] alive. Actors use detailed eye and hand movements, and one act can be stretched across many nights.

Not all theatre happened in grand buildings. Across India, folk forms like [[@yakshagana|Yakshagana]] in [[@karnataka|Karnataka]], Jatra in Bengal, Tamasha in Maharashtra and Nautanki in north India travelled from village to village. Every year, Ramlila performances act out the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]] in towns across north India, sometimes for weeks.

In London, Shakespeare's plays drew huge crowds to the Globe Theatre, built in 1599, where poorer people paid a penny to stand. In Japan, Noh theatre began in the 1300s and Kabuki in the 1600s. Today [[@broadway|Broadway]] in New York, London's West End and the theatres of Mumbai and [[@kolkata|Kolkata]] carry on the same old idea: people gathered in the dark, watching a story come alive.

text: Thiruvalluvar was a Tamil poet and thinker who wrote the [[@thirukkural|Tirukkural]], one of the most famous books in the Tamil language. It is a collection of 1,330 short couplets, two-line verses, giving advice on how to live a good life.
Nobody knows exactly when he lived. Guesses range from about 300 BCE to about 500 CE. Almost nothing reliable is known about his life either.

Yet his words are everywhere in Tamil Nadu. They are painted on buses, taught in schools, quoted in speeches and printed on calendars. People of different religions all find something in his book, because it talks about honesty, kindness and fairness without preaching a single faith.

st.prompt: The Tirukkural has three parts, on virtue, wealth and love. Which part is the longest?

options.t: Wealth, which covers rulers, ministers, friendship and work
Love, with stories of famous couples
Virtue, with rules for monks only

st.reveal: The part on wealth, called Porul, has 70 chapters, more than the other two put together. It covers how to rule fairly, choose good advisers and friends, and earn and spend money wisely.

myth: The Tirukkural is a holy book of one particular religion.
It names no god of any single religion and no particular sect. That is one reason people of many faiths, and none, have claimed it as their own.
facts: uncertain, somewhere between about 300 BCE and 500 CE

sec.t:
The Tirukkural is split into three parts. The first is about aram, or virtue: being truthful, patient and kind. The second, porul, is about wealth and public life: how kings should rule, how to choose friends and how to work hard. The third, inbam, is about love.

There are 133 chapters, each with exactly ten [[couplet|couplets]]. Every couplet is just seven Tamil words long. That makes them easy to remember, like a [[proverb|proverb]].

One well-known kural says, roughly, that the wound from fire may heal, but the wound from a harsh tongue never does. Another says that learning is the only wealth that never decays. These ideas still sound fresh today. Teachers in Tamil Nadu often ask children to learn a kural by heart, the way American students might learn a famous line from a speech.

Because so little is known, stories filled the gap. A popular tradition says Thiruvalluvar was a weaver who lived in Mylapore, in what is now [[@chennai|Chennai]]. Some stories give him a wife named Vasuki, who was famous for being patient and kind.

Historians treat these as legends, not facts. Even his name is a puzzle. "Thiru" is an honour, a little like "Shri". "Valluvar" may come from a community name, or simply mean someone who teaches.

Some scholars link the Tirukkural to the age of the [[@tamil-sangam|Tamil Sangam]] poets. Others think its language and ideas place it a few centuries later. They still debate this.

{{story:confucius}}

sec.h: A book for the whole world
sec.t:
The Tirukkural has been [[@translation|translated]] into dozens of languages, from English and Hindi to Russian and Japanese. Christian missionaries in the 1700s and 1800s were among the first to translate it into European languages.

Leo Tolstoy, the Russian writer, read parts of it in translation. In 1908 he quoted its lines on returning good for harm in a long essay called "A Letter to a Hindu". A young lawyer in South Africa named Mohandas Gandhi read that letter, printed it for Indian readers and later praised the Tirukkural himself.

Tamil Nadu honours him in many ways. Thiruvalluvar Day falls in mid-January, during the Pongal festival. In Chennai, a memorial called Valluvar Kottam, opened in 1976, is built in the shape of a temple chariot, with all 1,330 couplets carved on [[granite|granite]] panels.

The most dramatic memorial stands off [[@kanyakumari|Kanyakumari]], at the southern tip of India. On a small rock island, a stone statue of Thiruvalluvar rises 133 feet, about 40 m. It was unveiled on 1 January 2000.

The height is a code. The statue is 133 feet tall for the 133 chapters. Its base is 38 feet high, for the 38 chapters on virtue. The figure above stands 95 feet, for the chapters on wealth and love together. Waves crash below, and the statue looks out over the meeting of three seas. Since 2024 a glass-floored footbridge links it to the neighbouring Vivekananda Rock Memorial.

text: The spiral you see in a snail shell, a ram's horn, a [[hurricane|hurricane]] and a spiral [[galaxy|galaxy]] is usually a logarithmic spiral. It has a special property: each turn is a bigger copy of the one before, with exactly the same shape. Zoom in or out and it looks the same.

That is why it turns up everywhere. Anything that grows by adding a bit more on the outside, while keeping its shape, ends up drawing this curve. A shell can't rebuild its older inner rooms, so it adds bigger ones to the open end, and the spiral follows. The causes are different in different places, but the shape is the simplest answer to the same question.

st.prompt: Measure a real nautilus shell and compare how fast its spiral widens with the golden ratio (about 1.618). What do scientists usually find?

options.t: The shell grows more slowly, nearer 1.33 per turn-step, not golden
It matches 1.618 almost perfectly
It isn't a spiral at all

st.reveal: Shells measured by scientists follow a logarithmic spiral, but the growth factor varies and is usually well away from 1.618. The golden-shell story has been repeated in books and posters for over a century.

n.certNote: The logarithmic spiral really does appear across nature. Claims that shells and galaxies follow the golden ratio exactly are mostly myth, though sunflowers do use the golden angle.

d.try: Draw a dot in the middle of a page. Draw a line out from it in any direction, then turn the page a little and draw the next line slightly longer, always increasing by the same proportion, say 10 percent. Join the line ends and you will get a logarithmic spiral. Change the percentage to make it tighter or looser.
myth: Nautilus shells and spiral galaxies are perfect golden spirals.
Both are close to logarithmic spirals, but measurements show their growth rates vary and rarely match the golden ratio. The golden ratio does appear in the way many plants arrange seeds and leaves.
facts: it keeps exactly the same shape as it grows

sec.t:
You have probably seen posters of a nautilus shell with a golden rectangle drawn over it. The golden ratio, about 1.618, is a real and lovely number. A golden spiral is one particular logarithmic spiral that grows by that ratio every quarter turn.

The problem is that real nautilus shells don't match it. When scientists measure them, the shells widen more slowly, by roughly 1.33 for the same kind of step, and different shells vary. Galaxies vary even more, with some arms wound tightly and others loosely. Mathematician Mario Livio and others have spent years politely debunking the golden-shell story.

There is a true golden story, just in a different place. Look at the head of a sunflower and you will see two sets of spirals, one going clockwise and one anticlockwise. Count them and you usually get neighbouring [[@fibonacci-nature|Fibonacci numbers]], such as 34 and 55.

That happens because each new seed grows about 137.5 degrees round from the last one. This "golden angle" packs seeds as tightly as possible with no gaps. Pine cones, pineapples and cauliflowers show the same trick. It is one of the best examples of the [[@golden-ratio|golden ratio]] in nature.

In 2000, the American [[biologist|biologist]] Vance Tucker showed that falcons diving at prey fly in a logarithmic spiral. A falcon's sharpest vision looks out to the side, at an angle of about 40 degrees. If it turned its head to look straight ahead, the air resistance would slow it down. So it keeps its head straight and its eye fixed on the prey, which bends its path into a spiral.

That is the same rule that gives the spiral its other name, equiangular. The curve crosses every line from the centre at the same angle, just as the falcon keeps the same angle to its target. The [[@sky-peregrine|peregrine falcon]], fastest animal on Earth, is drawing maths as it dives.

[[@hurricanes|Hurricanes]] and spiral [[@galaxies|galaxies]] form their arms in very different ways from shells. A hurricane's cloud bands curve as air spins inward toward low pressure. Galaxy arms are waves of crowding, where stars and gas pile up as they [[orbit|orbit]], like a traffic jam on a ring road. Yet both end up close to logarithmic spirals, because that shape is what many spinning, growing systems settle into.

From a snail on a garden wall to a galaxy 100,000 [[lightyear|light-years]] across, the same curve keeps appearing. And patterns that repeat at every size have their own name and their own strange beauty, called [[@fractals|fractals]].

text: Zero and one behave in ways no other numbers do. Add 0 to any number, and the number stays the same. Multiply any number by 1, and it stays the same too. Multiply anything by 0, and you get 0. Mathematicians call 0 and 1 "identities", because they leave other numbers unchanged.

They are special for practical reasons as well. Zero is what lets us write big numbers with only ten digits, by holding empty places. And 0 and 1 together are enough to store anything a computer knows, from a selfie to a whole film.

st.prompt: What is 7 to the power of 0 (written 7⁰)?
st.reveal: Any number (except 0) to the power of 0 equals 1. Look at the pattern 7³ = 343, 7² = 49, 7¹ = 7. Each step divides by 7. One more step down gives 7 ÷ 7 = 1.

myth: Zero means nothing, so it doesn't really matter.
Zero holds places in numbers. Without it, 5, 50 and 500 would look the same. It also has its own rules. Adding it changes nothing, multiplying by it gives zero, and dividing by it has no answer.

sec.h: The number that holds a place
sec.t:
Many ancient peoples counted without zero. Roman numerals have no symbol for it. The Babylonians left a gap or used a mark to show an empty place, but didn't treat it as a number.

Indian mathematicians went further. In 628 CE, Brahmagupta wrote rules for zero as a number in its own right: a number minus itself is zero, and zero times anything is zero. At the Chaturbhuj temple in Gwalior, an [[inscription|inscription]] from 876 CE writes the number 270 with a small circle for zero, one of the oldest such zeros still on a wall. The Bakhshali [[manuscript|manuscript]], now in Oxford, uses a dot for zero, and some of its pages may be even older. These Indian [[@indian-numerals|numerals]] travelled through the Arab world to Europe.

Zero breaks one rule you learned early: you can always divide. What is 6 ÷ 0? If it had an answer, say x, then x × 0 would equal 6. But anything times 0 is 0. So there is no answer, and mathematicians say division by zero is "undefined". Calculators show an error.

People sometimes ask whether zero is even or odd. It's even, because it can be split into two equal groups of nothing, and it sits between the odd numbers −1 and 1.

Zero causes trouble outside maths too. Calendars jump from 1 BCE straight to 1 CE, with no year zero, because the system was set up in Europe before zero was in use there. In cricket, a batter out for 0 is said to be out for a "duck", because the 0 on the scoreboard looks like a duck's egg.

sec.h: Two numbers that run the world
sec.t:
Computers are built from billions of tiny switches that can be either off or on. Off is written 0 and on is written 1. A system that uses only these two digits is called [[@binary-code|binary]].

In [[binary|binary]], each place is worth double the one to its right: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and so on. So 1011 means 8 + 0 + 2 + 1, which is 11. String eight of these digits together and you can store any number from 0 to 255. Colours on a screen, letters in a message and notes in a song are all turned into long strings of 0s and 1s.

The German thinker Gottfried Leibniz wrote about binary in 1703. Centuries earlier, the Indian scholar Pingala had used patterns of short and long [[syllable|syllables]] in poetry that work in a similar way. Neither of them could have guessed that their two-symbol counting would one day carry video calls across the planet.

text: A marathon is 42.195 km because of the 1908 Olympics in London. The organisers planned a course from Windsor Castle to the new Olympic stadium at White City. To finish in front of the royal box, the race measured 26 miles and 385 yards, which is 42.195 km.
At first, marathons were all slightly different lengths, usually about 40 km. The 1908 distance became popular, and in 1921 the world athletics body made it the official length.

options.t: From Athens to Sparta, about 240 km, to ask for help
From Marathon to Athens, about 40 km, to announce victory
Around the walls of Athens three times

st.reveal: Herodotus, writing within a few decades of the battle, says Pheidippides ran to Sparta. The story of a run from Marathon to Athens, ending in his death, appears in writers who lived centuries later.

myth: The marathon is exactly the distance Pheidippides ran from Marathon to Athens.
The ancient run may never have happened, and early Olympic marathons were all different lengths. The exact 42.195 km comes from the course used at the 1908 London Olympics.

sec.t:
The race is named after Marathon, a plain in [[@ancient-greece|ancient Greece]] about 40 km from Athens. In 490 BCE, the Athenians defeated a Persian army there.

According to a famous story, a messenger ran all the way to Athens with the news, cried "We have won", then collapsed and died. But this version was written down by authors such as Plutarch and Lucian, who lived more than 500 years later. Herodotus, who wrote much closer to the time, tells of a runner called Pheidippides who ran about 240 km from Athens to Sparta to ask for help before the battle. Historians are not sure which story, if any, is true.

The marathon for the 1908 Olympics in [[@london|London]] started at Windsor Castle, so the royal children could watch. It ended in the stadium. Adding the extra yards to finish under the royal box gave 26 miles and 385 yards.

That race had a dramatic ending. Italian runner Dorando Pietri entered the stadium first but was so exhausted he fell several times. Officials helped him across the line, and he was disqualified. Queen Alexandra gave him a special gilded cup for his courage, and he became more famous than the winner.

Running 42 km is hard because of how the body stores energy. Muscles burn a fuel called glycogen, stored in muscles and the [[@liver|liver]]. Many runners run low on it after about 30 km. Their legs feel heavy and every step is a struggle, a feeling runners call "hitting the wall".

Marathon runners train for months and eat plenty of carbohydrate-rich [[@food-nutrients|food]], such as rice or pasta, before a race. During it, they drink and take energy gels to keep their [[@muscles|muscles]] going.

The [[@boston|Boston]] Marathon in the United States has been run every year since 1897. Women were not officially allowed to enter until 1972. In 1967 Kathrine Switzer entered as "K. V. Switzer" and finished, even after an official tried to pull her off the course. The first women's Olympic marathon was held in Los Angeles in 1984.

In 2023 Kelvin Kiptum of Kenya set the men's world record in Chicago, 2 hours 0 minutes 35 seconds. In April 2026 his countryman Sabastian Sawe ran 1 hour 59 minutes 30 seconds in London, the first time anyone had finished a marathon race in under two hours. In India, the [[@mumbai|Mumbai]] Marathon, first run in 2004, draws tens of thousands of runners each January, many in fancy dress, raising money for charity. Measuring a [[@measuring-units|kilometre]] exactly, through city streets, is a job for specialists who ride bikes with calibrated counters.

text: Yes, computers can produce pictures, music and poems, some of them good enough to win prizes or sell for large sums. Whether that counts as art is a harder question, and people genuinely disagree.

Most of today's art programs are a kind of [[@ai-what|artificial intelligence]]. They are trained on millions of pictures, each with a caption. From those, the program learns which shapes, colours and textures tend to go with words like "sunset", "elephant" or "watercolour". Give it a new sentence and it produces a new picture to match. It has never seen a sunset itself. It has only seen what people photographed and painted.

st.prompt: Many AI image programs start each new picture from something surprising. What is it?

options.t: A screen full of random speckles, like TV static
A blank white canvas
A random painting copied from the internet

st.reveal: Most popular image generators begin with pure noise. Then, over many small steps, they nudge the speckles towards something that matches your words, the way a photo slowly comes into focus.

n.certNote: Computers can clearly produce striking pictures, music and poems. Whether that counts as art, who the artist is, and whether training on human artists' work is fair are all still argued over by artists, lawyers and philosophers.

Give the same line to three friends or family members and ask each to draw it in five minutes. Compare the drawings and talk about which choices each person made that the words didn't say.

Most generators don't stitch together pieces of stored images. They learn patterns from millions of pictures and then produce new pixels. Even so, they can sometimes produce something very close to a famous image they saw often during training.

sec.t:
Computer art is older than most people think. In the early 1970s, a British painter named Harold Cohen began writing a program called AARON. He taught it rules about shapes, bodies and plants, and it drew pictures with a robotic pen. Later it chose colours too. Cohen kept improving it until he died in 2016.

Cohen never claimed AARON was an artist on its own. He saw it more like a very unusual paintbrush, one that could surprise its maker. Many artists who use AI today describe their work in a similar way.

sec.h: The portrait that shocked an auction
sec.t:
In 2018, the auction house Christie's in New York sold a blurry portrait of a made-up gentleman called Edmond de Belamy. A group of young French artists had made it using an AI program trained on thousands of old portraits. It sold for $432,500, far above the expected price.

Some people called it a turning point. Others pointed out that the code the group used had been written mostly by someone else, and shared freely online. That argument, about who really made the picture, has followed AI art ever since.

Many illustrators and painters are upset that their work was used to train AI programs without their permission and without payment. Some have taken companies to court in the US and elsewhere. The companies argue that learning from public images is allowed, the way a student learns by looking at [[@famous-paintings|famous paintings]]. Courts have not settled the matter yet.

There is also the question of ownership. In 2023, the US Copyright Office said that pictures made entirely by AI cannot be copyrighted, because copyright protects work by a human author. If a person makes real creative choices, such as arranging, editing or painting over, those human parts can be protected.

People have asked "is it art?" many times before. When photography appeared in the 1800s, some painters said a machine couldn't make art. Later, critics said the same about [[@modern-art|modern art]] that didn't look like anything. Each time, people slowly worked out new ideas about what an artist does. Many think the same will happen again: the thinking, choosing and meaning may matter more than who, or what, holds the brush.

text: A neural network is a computer program built from lots of tiny maths units, called artificial [[neuron|neurons]], joined together in layers. Each unit takes in some numbers, multiplies them by its own settings, adds them up and passes the result on. Alone, a unit does almost nothing. Millions of them working together can learn to recognise faces, translate languages or spot a disease in an X-ray.

The name comes from the [[@brain-works|neurons in your brain]], which pass signals to one another. A neural network is a very rough copy of that idea. What makes it special is that nobody writes the rules for it. It learns them from examples.

st.prompt: A neural network trained only on photos of dogs in parks is shown a dog on a beach. What might go wrong?

options.t: It may fail, because it learned to look for grass instead of the dog
Nothing, it understands what a dog is
It will say the beach is a dog

st.reveal: Networks learn whatever patterns help them guess right in training, and sometimes that is the background, not the animal. If every dog photo had grass, grass may become part of its idea of "dog". This is why good training data needs lots of variety.

d.try: Play "human neural network" with three friends. One person sees a picture and may only say one word to the next, who passes one word to the last, who must guess the picture. Swap roles after each round and notice how you all get better at choosing useful words.
myth: A neural network works just like a human brain.

It borrows a simple idea from the brain, that many small units passing signals can learn together. Real neurons are far more complicated, and a brain learns from far fewer examples than most networks need.
facts: Learns by adjusting millions or billions of numbers called weights

sec.t:
A typical network has an input layer, several hidden layers and an output layer. Say you want it to tell cats from dogs. A photo goes in as a grid of numbers, one for each pixel's colour.

The first layer might react to simple things, like edges and patches of colour. Later layers combine those into shapes: an ear, an eye, a whisker. The last layer adds everything up and gives two numbers, how likely the picture is a cat and how likely it is a dog. No one tells the network to look for ears. It finds that ears are useful by itself.

sec.h: A slow start, then a rush
sec.t:
The idea is old. In 1943, Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts described an artificial neuron using maths. In 1958, Frank Rosenblatt built the perceptron, a machine that could learn to sort simple shapes. Newspapers got very excited, then disappointed, as early networks hit their limits.

For decades, computers were too slow and there wasn't enough data. That changed with the internet, which provided millions of labelled photos, and with graphics chips designed for video games, which turned out to be very good at this kind of maths. In 2012, a network called AlexNet beat every other method at recognising objects in photos by a wide margin. After that, neural networks spread almost everywhere.

If your phone opens when it sees your face, a neural network is doing [[@face-recognition|face recognition]]. Networks suggest the next word as you type, clean up blurry photos, translate menus and help doctors read scans. Weather forecasters and [[astronomer|astronomers]] use them too.

The chatbots that answer questions in full sentences are built from very large neural networks trained on huge amounts of text. They are called [[@large-language-models|large language models]], and some have hundreds of billions of weights.

A neural network only knows the patterns in its training data. If the examples are narrow or unfair, the network will be too. One trained mostly on light-skinned faces may perform worse on darker-skinned ones, a problem researchers have found in real systems.

Networks also can't easily explain their answers. You can see millions of weights, but not a neat list of reasons. That makes people careful about using them for big decisions, like medical treatment or who gets a loan. Many researchers now work on making them easier to check.

text: The East India Company was a business set up by London merchants in 1600 to trade in Asian [[@spices|spices]]. Queen Elizabeth I gave it a [[monopoly|monopoly]], the sole right among the English, to trade east of Africa.

In India, it built trading posts at Surat, Madras, Bombay and Calcutta, buying cotton cloth, indigo, saltpetre and later tea. As the [[@mughals|Mughal]] Empire weakened in the 1700s, the Company built its own army of Indian soldiers. In 1757 it won the [[@plassey|Battle of Plassey]] in Bengal, and in 1765 it gained the right to collect taxes in Bengal, Bihar and Odisha. Over the next 90 years it took over most of India by war, [[treaty|treaties]] and annexation. After the revolt of 1857, the British government took control and the Company was later shut down.

st.prompt: In 1765, the Mughal emperor gave the Company the "diwani" of Bengal, Bihar and Odisha. What was that?

options.t: The right to collect the land taxes
The right to build a church
Permission to sell tea

st.reveal: The diwani was the right to collect revenue, mostly land tax, from the richest provinces of India. Suddenly a trading company had a government's income. It used that money to buy Indian goods and pay for its army.

d.try: Play a simple trading game with a friend. Each of you starts with ten buttons or beads and some "goods", such as pencils or stickers, and trades for a few minutes. Then give one player the right to "collect tax" of one bead from every trade, and see how fast the balance changes.
myth: The British government conquered India from the start.
For about 100 years, it was a private company, with shareholders in London, that conquered and ruled large parts of India. The British government took over directly only in 1858.
facts: Rule handed to the British Crown

sec.t:
The Company's first ships reached India in 1608. In 1613 the emperor Jahangir allowed it to open a trading post, called a factory, at Surat in Gujarat. An English ambassador, Sir Thomas Roe, spent years at Jahangir's court seeking better terms.

At first, the Company was one trader among many, competing with the Portuguese, [[@dutch-french-india|the Dutch and later the French]]. It needed Indian goods far more than India needed English ones. European buyers loved Indian cotton cloth, especially light printed calicoes and chintz.

In 1756, the young Nawab of Bengal, Siraj ud-Daulah, captured Calcutta. A year later, Company troops under Robert Clive met his much larger army at Plassey, now Palashi.

Clive had secretly agreed with the Nawab's commander, Mir Jafar, to make him Nawab if he held his troops back. Mir Jafar did, and the Company won easily. In 1765, after another victory at Buxar, the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II granted the Company the right to collect revenue in Bengal, Bihar and Odisha.

The Company now had a government's income. By around 1800, its army had grown to roughly 2 lakh soldiers, most of them Indian [[sepoy|sepoys]]. It fought and defeated Mysore under [[@tipu-sultan|Tipu Sultan]], the [[@marathas|Marathas]] and the Sikh kingdom of Punjab.

Its rule brought heavy taxes, and many officials grew rich. In 1770, a terrible [[famine|famine]] struck Bengal, and millions died while tax collection continued. In Britain, critics in Parliament attacked the Company's greed. The Company also introduced new courts, surveys, railways and the [[@telegraph|telegraph]], mainly to help its own rule and trade.

In 1857, Indian soldiers rose up in a great [[@revolt-1857|revolt]] that spread across north India. It was crushed, but it shocked Britain.

In 1858, Parliament took India away from the Company and placed it directly under the British Crown. The Company carried on as a small business for a few years and was closed in 1874. Its story left behind cities, laws and railways, and English words such as "loot", "jungle" and "shampoo", borrowed from Indian languages.

text: Yes. Walk down a street in Pompeii in AD 79 and you would pass a snack bar every few minutes. The Romans called it a *thermopolium*, which roughly means "place that sells hot things". It had a stone counter facing the street, with big clay jars sunk into the top to keep stews, beans and wine warm. You pointed, paid, and ate standing up or walking away.

[[archaeologist|Archaeologists]] have found around 80 of these counters in [[@pompeii|Pompeii]], a town of maybe 11,000 people. That is more snack bars per person than many modern towns have burger joints.

st.prompt: Scientists tested food scraps in the jars of a Pompeii snack bar. Which of these did they find?

options.t: Duck, pig, goat, fish and snails
Potatoes and tomatoes
Only bread and water

st.reveal: Traces of duck, pork, goat, fish and land snails turned up in the jars and on the counter. Potatoes and tomatoes come from the Americas, so no Roman ever ate them.

src: Pompeii Archaeological Park (Parco Archeologico di Pompei), Regio V excavations.

src.Mary Beard, Pompeii: The Life of a Roman Town (2008).

n.certNote: How many snack bars Pompeii had depends on how archaeologists count a shop. Estimates run from about 80 to over 150.

myth: Fast food is a modern invention that began with American burger chains.
Cities have sold ready-to-eat food for thousands of years. Roman towns had snack counters on busy streets, and Chinese cities had night markets selling noodles and dumplings a thousand years ago.

sec.h: The snack bar with ducks on the counter
sec.t:
In 2019, diggers in a part of Pompeii called Regio V uncovered a counter that still had its paint. Bright pictures covered the front: two ducks hanging upside down, ready for the pot, a rooster, and a dog on a lead. The pictures were probably a menu. A picture of a duck meant duck was for sale.

Inside the jars, scientists found tiny bits of duck bone, pork, goat, fish and snails. One jar held ground fava beans, which Romans sometimes added to wine to change its colour and taste. The volcano's ash had sealed everything in place, like a lunchbox nobody opened for 2,000 years.

A Roman snack bar sold food you could eat fast: lentil and bean stews, porridge, sausages, cheese, olives, flat bread, and boiled eggs. Wine was usually mixed with water, sometimes served warm with spices.

Almost everything came with garum, a salty sauce made by leaving fish and salt in the sun for weeks until it broke down. That sounds gross, but it is close to the fish sauce still used in Thai and Vietnamese cooking. It works through [[@fermentation|fermentation]], the same process that turns milk into curd.

Missing from the menu? Tomatoes, potatoes, chillies and corn. Those all came from the Americas, and Europe didn't see them until about 1,500 years later.

Roman leaders didn't always trust these places. Crowds gathered there, drank, gambled and talked about politics. The writer Suetonius says that Emperor Nero once banned snack bars from selling cooked food, except beans and vegetables. Rules like that came and went, and the counters kept serving.

Rome was not alone. In China, around a thousand years ago, the city of Kaifeng had night markets where stalls sold noodles, dumplings and grilled meat until late. In India, travellers' accounts describe sellers of ready-cooked food at markets and pilgrim towns for many centuries. Wherever crowds gathered and people worked long hours, someone set up a stove and sold a quick meal.

Only about two-thirds of Pompeii has been dug up. Every few years, archaeologists find another counter, another painted wall, another kitchen pot. Life in towns across [[@ancient-rome|ancient Rome]] is easier to picture because of finds like these. And the best clues sit right beside the counters: customers waiting for their stew scratched jokes, prices and insults into the plaster, and that [[@oddity-ancient-graffiti|Roman graffiti]] can still be read today.

text: Sikhism began in Punjab about 500 years ago with [[@guru-nanak|Guru Nanak]]. He taught that there is one God, that all people are equal and that ordinary family life can be holy. Over the next two centuries, nine more Gurus, or spiritual teachers, led the Sikh community in turn.

Each Guru added something. Some built towns and temples, one compiled the holy book, and two were killed by Mughal authorities for refusing to give up their beliefs. The tenth, Guru Gobind Singh, founded the Khalsa, the community of initiated Sikhs, and declared that after him the holy book itself, the [[@guru-granth-sahib|Guru Granth Sahib]], would be the eternal Guru.

st.prompt: Before he died in 1708, Guru Gobind Singh named who would be the next Guru?

options.t: The holy book, the Guru Granth Sahib
His eldest surviving son
The Sikh with the most votes in Anandpur

st.reveal: Guru Gobind Singh declared that there would be no more human Gurus. The scripture would be the Guru from then on. That is why Sikhs show the Guru Granth Sahib the respect given to a living teacher.

myth: Sikhism is a mix of Hinduism and Islam.

Sikhism is a separate religion with its own scripture, Gurus, beliefs and practices. Its holy book does include poems by Hindu and Muslim saints whose ideas the Gurus admired, but Sikhs see their faith as its own revelation.

sec.h: Guru Nanak and the open kitchen
sec.t:
Guru Nanak was born in 1469 at Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib in Pakistan. He travelled widely, perhaps as far as Mecca and Sri Lanka, singing hymns with his Muslim companion Mardana, who played the rabab, a stringed instrument.

He taught that God cannot be divided by religion or caste. In his last years he settled at Kartarpur, where his followers farmed, prayed and ate together. The free community kitchen, called *langar*, became a lasting Sikh tradition. Rich and poor, of any faith or caste, sit side by side and eat the same food.

sec.h: Two swords and a child Guru
sec.t:
The sixth Guru, Guru Hargobind, began wearing two swords: one for spiritual authority and one for worldly authority. He built the Akal Takht, a seat of Sikh authority, facing the Harmandir Sahib.

The seventh, Guru Har Rai, is remembered for his gentleness and for keeping a garden of healing herbs. The eighth, Guru Har Krishan, became Guru as a small child. During a smallpox outbreak in Delhi in 1664, he is said to have cared for the sick before falling ill and dying himself, aged just seven. Gurdwara Bangla Sahib in Delhi stands on the site.

The ninth Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur, was executed in Delhi in 1675 on the orders of the emperor Aurangzeb. Sikh tradition says he gave his life defending the right of Kashmiri Hindus to practise their faith. Gurdwara Sis Ganj in Chandni Chowk marks the spot.

His son, Guru Gobind Singh, was a poet and warrior. On Vaisakhi in 1699, at Anandpur Sahib, he founded the Khalsa. Its members were asked to keep five articles of faith, including uncut hair and a steel bracelet. Men took the name Singh and women the name Kaur, so that no surname could show caste. He lost all four of his sons in the struggles with Mughal forces.

Before his death in 1708, Guru Gobind Singh ended the line of human Gurus. The Guru Granth Sahib became the Guru. Sikhs read from it, sing its hymns and treat it with great respect, carrying it to rest each night. Today there are around 25–30 million Sikhs, in Punjab and in [[@indian-diaspora|communities around the world]], from Canada and the UK to California.

text: The Sumerians lived in southern Mesopotamia, the flat land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers in what is now Iraq. From about 3500 BCE they built some of the world's first cities, with temples, markets, schools and thousands of people living close together.

They are best known for one of the oldest writing systems on Earth, called cuneiform. They also developed counting in sixties, built huge stepped temples called ziggurats and wrote early laws, poems and epics. Their language died out more than 3,000 years ago, but some of their ideas still shape how we tell the time.

st.prompt: The earliest Sumerian writing was used mainly for one thing. What was it?

options.t: Keeping track of goods like grain, sheep and beer
Writing down stories about gods and heroes
Sending love letters

st.reveal: The first clay tablets from Uruk are mostly lists and accounts for temple stores. Stories, laws, letters and poems came later, once scribes realised the same marks could record speech.

d.try: Roll out a flat slab of clay or play dough. Use the end of a lolly stick or a chopstick, cut at an angle, to press wedge-shaped marks into it. Invent symbols for three things in your house, like a cup or a book, and "write" a list of how many you have. You've made your own cuneiform tablet.
myth: Writing was invented so people could record stories and history.
In Sumer, writing grew out of bookkeeping. Officials needed to track who owed what to the temples. Literature came centuries later.
facts: southern Mesopotamia, in today's southern Iraq

sec.t:
Southern Mesopotamia had rich soil but very little rain, no stone and hardly any trees. The Sumerians solved this with mud. They dug canals to carry river water to fields of barley and wheat, and they shaped mud into bricks for houses, walls and temples.

Farming grew so well that not everyone had to farm. Some people became priests, potters, metalworkers, traders or soldiers. Villages grew into cities. By about 3000 BCE, Uruk may have held 40,000 people or more, making it one of the largest cities in the world at the time.

Each city had its own ruler and its own god. The cities often traded with each other and just as often fought over water and land.

sec.h: Sixty minutes and a game board
sec.t:
The Sumerians counted in groups of 60. Sixty is handy because it divides evenly by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30. Later peoples in Mesopotamia passed this system on, and it survives in our 60-second minutes, 60-minute hours and 360-degree circles, all part of how we [[@time-measure|measure time]].

In the 1920s, the British [[archaeologist|archaeologist]] Leonard Woolley dug up the Royal Cemetery at Ur. Among gold helmets, jewellery and harps decorated with bulls' heads, his team found a beautiful game board inlaid with shell and stone. Today it's called the Royal Game of Ur. Using a clay tablet from much later, a British Museum curator worked out how it was probably played, and people [[@board-games|play it again]] today.

Sumer had few raw materials, so it traded far and wide. Sumerian texts mention ships arriving from a land called Meluhha, carrying carnelian beads, timber, ivory and gold. Most historians think Meluhha was the Indus Valley [[civilisation|civilisation]]. Indus-style seals and beads have turned up in Mesopotamian cities, evidence of the [[@harappan-trade|Harappan trade]] network that linked the two great river cultures.

Around 2300 BCE, Sargon of Akkad, from just north of Sumer, conquered its cities and built one of the first [[empire|empires]]. He made his daughter Enheduanna high priestess at Ur. She wrote hymns to the moon god and the goddess Inanna, and she is often described as the earliest author known by name.

Sumerian cities rose again under the kings of Ur, who built its great ziggurat around 2100 BCE. Its lower levels still stand near Nasiriyah in Iraq. About 2000 BCE, Ur was sacked and Sumer faded. Scribes kept copying the Sumerian language for centuries, much as Europeans later used Latin, long after anyone spoke it at home.

text: The Maldives is a country of about 1,190 small coral islands in the Indian Ocean, south-west of India and Sri Lanka. The islands are grouped into 26 rings called [[atoll|atolls]]. Its land is flat and very low: about 80 percent of it lies less than a metre above sea level, and the highest natural point is only about 2.4 metres. No country on Earth is lower.

That makes it extremely sensitive to [[@sea-level-rise|sea level rise]]. As the planet warms, ice on land melts and seawater expands, slowly lifting the ocean. Even a rise of half a metre would mean more flooding, salty water in wells and [[@sand-where|beaches]] washing away. Scientists expect the sea to rise somewhere between about 30 centimetres and a metre by 2100, depending on how much pollution the world produces.

st.prompt: Much of the white sand on Maldivian beaches comes from an unusual source. What is it?

options.t: Parrotfish, which bite off coral and grind it up
Sand blown across the sea from deserts
Crushed volcanic rock

st.reveal: Parrotfish scrape algae off coral with beak-like teeth, swallowing bits of coral as they go. They grind it up and pass it out as fine white sand. Studies in the Maldives found parrotfish make a large share of the sand that builds up the islands.

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Maldives.

Maldives Bureau of Statistics, Census 2022.
n.certNote: Sea level is rising, and that is well measured. How fast it will rise by 2100 depends on future pollution, and scientists are still studying whether healthy coral reefs can build islands up fast enough to keep pace.

myth: The Maldives are sinking.

The islands themselves are not sinking. The sea around them is slowly rising. Coral islands can even grow, as reefs make new sand, but scientists worry that the sea may rise faster than healthy reefs can keep up.

sec.t:
The Maldives sits on top of an underwater mountain range. Over millions of years, [[@coral-reefs|coral reefs]] grew on the old volcanic peaks, in rings near the surface. Waves broke off bits of coral and shells and piled them up as sandbanks, which slowly became islands with palm trees.

Much of the white sand has a funny source: parrotfish. They nibble [[algae|algae]] off the coral with tough beaks and grind up the coral as they go, then pass it out as sand. A single big parrotfish can make hundreds of kilograms of sand a year.

The word for these rings, "atoll", came into English from Dhivehi, the language of the Maldives. It is one of many [[@words-borrowed|borrowed words]] in English that started life in South Asia.

{{story:coral-bleaching}}

In October 2009, President Mohamed Nasheed and his ministers put on scuba gear and held a cabinet meeting on the seabed, about 6 metres down. They signed a letter calling on all countries to cut the gases that cause [[@climate-change|climate change]]. The pictures went around the world.

For the Maldives, warming oceans bring a second danger. When the sea gets too hot, corals push out the tiny algae that live inside them, turn white and may die. This happened across the Maldives in 1998 and again in 2016. Without living coral, there is no new sand, and the reefs that break the force of waves get weaker.

The capital, Malé, packs well over a lakh of people onto an island of about 2 square kilometres, one of the most crowded places on Earth. A sea wall surrounds it. In December 2004, the Indian Ocean [[@tsunami|tsunami]] flooded much of the city and many other islands.

Next to Malé, the government has built a new island called Hulhumalé by pumping sand from the [[lagoon|lagoon]] onto a reef. It stands about 2 metres above sea level, higher than most natural islands, and tens of thousands of people already live there. Other ideas include floating homes and moving people to a few bigger, raised islands.

Most Maldivians are Muslim and speak Dhivehi, written in a script called Thaana that runs from right to left. Fishing for tuna, often with poles and lines rather than big nets, has fed families for centuries. Today tourism is the biggest business. Many resorts take up a whole island each, with wooden villas on stilts over the lagoon.

text: Cairo is the biggest city in the Arab world and one of the largest in Africa, home to about 2.2 crore people in its greater area (2024 estimate). That is about as many as live in and around Mumbai. It sits on the River Nile, where the green river valley opens into the wide delta, with desert pressing in on both sides.

Today's Cairo is a city of honking traffic, rooftop gardens, ancient mosques, glass towers and markets that have been trading for 600 years. And the [[@pyramids|pyramids]] of Giza are not far away in the desert. They are on the edge of town.

st.reveal: Cairo has hundreds of mosques, many centuries old, and their tall towers, called minarets, rise all over the old city. From a rooftop at sunset you can hear the call to prayer echoing from dozens of them at once.

myth: The pyramids stand alone in the middle of an empty desert.
The Giza pyramids sit right at the edge of a huge city. Houses, roads and even a pizza shop look straight at the Sphinx, and the desert begins only on the far side.
