sec.h: A city on a strip of green
sec.t:
From space, Egypt looks like a brown sheet with one green ribbon running down it. That ribbon is the [[@egypt-nile|Nile]], and Cairo is the knot at the top. Almost all Egyptians live within a few kilometres of the river, because everywhere else is desert.

Cairo gets about 25 mm of rain in a whole year. Some years it barely rains at all. Every glass of water, every field of beans and every swimming pool depends on the Nile. Its water fell as rain thousands of kilometres away, in the mountains of Ethiopia and East Africa.

sec.h: Old Cairo and very old Cairo
sec.t:
The pyramids are about 4,500 years old, but the city of Cairo itself is much younger. It was founded in AD 969 by the Fatimid rulers, who named it *al-Qahira*, "the victorious". Its Al-Azhar mosque, begun soon after, has been a centre of Islamic learning for over 1,000 years.

Old Cairo has so many mosques that people call it the city of a thousand [[minaret|minarets]]. The Khan el-Khalili market dates back to the 1380s. Its narrow lanes sell spices, brass lamps, perfume bottles and tiny cups of sweet mint tea.

Further south lies Coptic Cairo, home to some of Egypt's oldest churches. The Hanging Church gets its name because it was built on top of the gatehouse of an old Roman [[fortress|fortress]], so its floor seems to float above the ground. Egypt's Christians, called Copts, make up roughly a tenth of the country's people.

{{story:hieroglyphs}}

sec.h: A brand-new museum for very old treasures
sec.t:
For over a century, Egypt's greatest treasures were crammed into a pink building in central Cairo. In November 2025, the Grand Egyptian Museum opened in full beside the Giza plateau. It is the largest museum in the world for a single [[civilisation|civilisation]].

For the first time, all of Tutankhamun's treasures are shown together, about 5,000 objects, from his golden mask to his sandals. A giant statue of Ramesses II, as tall as a four-storey house, greets visitors in the entrance hall. In 2018 it was carried there on a special truck, crawling through the streets at walking pace.

Cairo's metro opened in 1987, the first in Africa. Its lines carry millions of people a day, and some carriages are set aside for women only. Above ground, microbuses, tuk-tuks and taxis squeeze through some of the busiest roads anywhere.

To ease the crowding, Egypt is building a New Administrative Capital about 45 km east of Cairo, with government buildings, a huge mosque and Africa's tallest skyscraper. Many ministries have already moved there.

On the eastern edge of Cairo lives a community called the Zabbaleen, which means "garbage people". For decades they have collected rubbish from homes across the city by donkey cart and truck, then sorted it by hand. They reuse or sell a huge share of it, far more than many official [[@recycling|recycling]] systems manage.

The city is old, new and noisy all at once. And under its streets and suburbs, [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] keep finding tombs, which is why every new building project in Cairo might turn into a dig for [[@mummies|mummies]].

text: About a quarter of the Netherlands lies below sea level, and much more would flood if rivers burst their banks. The Dutch live there safely because, for about a thousand years, they have built walls of earth called dikes to hold back the sea and rivers. Then they pump the water out from behind them.

Land won back from water like this is called a polder. Pumps run day and night to keep polders dry. On top of that, giant storm barriers can shut the sea out during storms. It is a constant job, and the Dutch have whole local governments devoted to it.

st.prompt: Before electric pumps, how did the Dutch keep water out of land below sea level?

options.t: They carried it out in buckets
Windmills turned wheels and screws that lifted water into higher canals
They let it evaporate in the sun

st.reveal: Many of the famous Dutch windmills were really water pumps. Their sails turned paddle wheels or giant screws that lifted water step by step into higher channels and rivers, until it could flow out to sea.

myth: The story of the little Dutch boy with his finger in the dike is an old Dutch legend.

It first appeared in a French children's story in 1848 and then in English magazines. It became world famous through Hans Brinker, or the Silver Skates, a novel by the American writer Mary Mapes Dodge published in 1865. The Dutch didn't know the tale until tourists began asking about it. A statue of the boy was later put up to please visitors.

sec.t:
The western Netherlands began as marshes, peat bogs and river mouths. Around a thousand years ago, farmers started digging ditches to drain the bogs. But drained peat shrinks and sinks. The more they drained, the lower the land became, and the more they needed dikes.

So the Dutch got very good at moving water. Today the lowest point, near Rotterdam, is about 6.7 m below sea level. Standing there, the sea would be higher than a two-storey house.

Many of the famous Dutch windmills were not for grinding grain. They were pumps. Their sails turned paddle wheels or big screws that lifted water out of ditches into higher canals. Several windmills in a row could raise water step by step.

At Kinderdijk, near Rotterdam, 19 windmills built mostly around 1740 still stand in neat lines. They are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Today electric pumping stations do the hard work, but the old mills still spin. Their great-grandchildren are the [[@wind-turbines|wind turbines]] now spinning off the Dutch coast.

sec.h: The night the sea came in
sec.t:
On the night of 31 January 1953, a huge storm pushed the North Sea against the southwest of the country. Dikes broke in many places. About 1,800 people in the Netherlands died, and tens of thousands of animals drowned.

The country vowed it would never happen again. It built the Delta Works, a chain of dams, sluices and storm barriers that took decades to finish. One of them, the Maeslantkering near Rotterdam, has two floating arms, each about 210 m long, about as long as two football fields. In a big storm they swing shut across the river to block the sea.

sec.h: A whole province from the sea
sec.t: In 1932, the Dutch finished the Afsluitdijk, a sea dam about 32 km long. It turned a stormy saltwater bay into a calm freshwater lake. Then they built polders inside it. One of them became the province of Flevoland, where more than 400,000 people now live on land that was seabed a hundred years ago.

India has its own polder country. In [[@kerala|Kerala]], much of the Kuttanad region lies between about 1 and 3 m below sea level. Farmers there have grown rice behind mud walls for centuries, pumping water out of their fields. The United Nations food agency has recognised it as a globally important farming system.

Both places now face the same worry. Warmer oceans and melting ice are slowly raising the seas, as you can see in [[@sea-level-rise|sea level rise]]. The Dutch are now giving some land back to rivers, so floodwater has room to spread safely.

text: For hundreds of millions of Hindus, Krishna is a god, believed to be a form of Vishnu who came to Earth. The stories of his childhood are some of the best loved in India. They are told mainly in the Bhagavata Purana, a long Sanskrit text, and also in the Harivamsa and the Vishnu Purana.

In these stories, young Krishna is a cheeky cowherd boy. He steals [[@butter-ghee|butter]], plays the flute, teases the village girls and outwits demons sent to kill him. Grandparents tell the tales at bedtime, temples act them out, and painters, poets and dancers have retold them for well over a thousand years.

st.reveal: The Bhagavata Purana says the storm lasted seven days and nights, and Krishna held the hill up on one finger the whole time. The villagers and their cows sheltered underneath until the rain god Indra gave up.

myth: Krishna is shown blue because the stories say his skin was blue.
Many old texts describe him as dark, using words like "shyama" or comparing him to a rain cloud. Painters chose blue as a way to show that deep, cloudy darkness, and the colour stuck.

sec.h: A baby smuggled through a storm
sec.t:
The story begins with a frightening prophecy. King Kamsa of Mathura hears that the eighth child of his sister Devaki will kill him. So he locks Devaki and her husband Vasudeva in prison.

When Krishna, the eighth child, is born at midnight, the guards fall asleep and the doors swing open. Vasudeva carries the newborn in a basket across the flooded Yamuna river. In many tellings, a great serpent spreads its hoods over the baby like an umbrella. Krishna is left with the cowherd Nanda and his wife Yashoda in Gokul, who raise him as their son. His birthday is celebrated every year as Janmashtami, with midnight prayers and cradles decorated with flowers.

sec.h: Snakes, storms and a lifted hill
sec.t:
Young Krishna also faces danger. The demoness Putana tries to poison him and fails. The many-headed serpent Kaliya poisons the river, so Krishna jumps in and dances on its heads until it leaves.

The most famous tale is about Govardhan hill. When the villagers stop offering prayers to Indra, the rain god, he sends a seven-day storm. Krishna lifts the whole hill on one finger, and the village shelters beneath it like a giant umbrella. Pilgrims still walk the roughly 21-kilometre path around Govardhan hill near Mathura.

sec.h: A flute heard across the arts
sec.t:
Krishna's flute, his peacock feather and his cows appear everywhere in Indian art. Painters in the hills of Kangra showed him in soft greens and blues, and [[@kangra-painting|Kangra paintings]] are still famous for it. The 16th-century poet Surdas wrote hundreds of songs about Krishna as a child, often from Yashoda's point of view.

In Braj, the region around Mathura and Vrindavan, [[@holi|Holi]] lasts for days because of stories of Krishna playing with colours. Dances such as Manipuri retell his circle dance with the gopis, the village girls.

Krishna does not stay in Vrindavan. He returns to Mathura, defeats Kamsa and later becomes a king. As an adult, he is a key figure in the [[epic|epic]] [[@mahabharata|Mahabharata]], where he guides the warrior Arjuna. And the strangest part? The same butter-stealing boy is the teacher who speaks the [[@bhagavad-gita|Bhagavad Gita]], one of the most read religious texts in the world.

text: Goan food is a mix of Konkan coastal cooking and about 450 years of Portuguese rule. The everyday meal is fish curry and rice, flavoured with coconut and the sour fruit kokum. On top of that, the Portuguese brought vinegar-based dishes, pork, bread, and ingredients from the Americas such as [[@chillies|chillies]], cashews and potatoes.

The result is food found nowhere else in India: tangy vindaloo, spicy sorpotel, green cafreal chicken, crusty bread rolls and a layered sweet called bebinca. Goan Hindu and Goan Catholic families each have their own cooking traditions, which share many flavours.

st.prompt: Where does the word "vindaloo" come from?

options.t: A Portuguese dish of meat in wine vinegar and garlic
The Hindi word "aloo", because it contains potatoes
A village in Goa where it was first cooked

st.reveal: Vindaloo comes from the Portuguese "carne de vinha d'alhos", meat in wine and garlic. In Goa, cooks used palm vinegar and added chillies and spices, creating a new dish. Traditional vindaloo has no potatoes at all.

myth: Vindaloo is a potato curry, because its name has "aloo" in it.
The name comes from the Portuguese "vinha d'alhos", meaning wine and garlic. Traditional Goan vindaloo is made with pork and has no potatoes. The "aloo" is a coincidence.

sec.t:
Goa sits on India's west coast, where rivers meet the Arabian Sea. Fish is part of almost every meal. A typical Goan fish curry uses coconut ground with [[@food-why-chillies-red|red chillies]], coriander and turmeric, soured with kokum or [[@tamarind|tamarind]].

Mackerel, kingfish, prawns and pomfret are favourites. Fishing boats bring the catch to beaches and markets early in the morning, and the fish is often cooked the same day. During the [[monsoon|monsoon]], when fishing at sea pauses, families rely more on dried fish stored earlier in the year. Goans eat their curry with boiled red rice, often with fried fish on the side. For many Goans, "xit kodi" (rice and curry in Konkani) is simply what lunch means.

Vindaloo began as the Portuguese "carne de vinha d'alhos", meat soaked in wine and garlic. In Goa, cooks replaced the wine with palm vinegar, added dried red chillies and spices, and made it their own. It's traditionally made with pork.

Sorpotel is a spicy pork dish that tastes better after a few days, so it's often made before [[@christmas|Christmas]]. Xacuti is a rich curry with roasted coconut and many spices. Cafreal is chicken coated in a green paste of coriander, chillies and spices, then fried. Its name is linked to Portuguese soldiers from Africa.

Before the Portuguese, Goans ate mostly rice. The Portuguese brought wheat bread, and Goan bakers called poders learned to make it. Many still cycle through villages in the mornings with baskets of fresh bread, honking a horn.

Goan breads include pão (soft rolls), poi (a round bread with bran) and kankonn, a crisp ring-shaped bread. From Goa, soft rolls spread to Mumbai, where they became the pav in vada pav and pav bhaji.

Bebinca is Goa's best-known dessert. It's made from coconut milk, eggs, sugar and flour, baked one thin layer at a time. A traditional bebinca can have seven to sixteen layers and takes hours to make.

At Christmas, Catholic families make plates of sweets called kuswar, including neureos, filled pastries, and dodol, a dark sweet made with coconut and [[@jaggery|jaggery]]. Goan Hindu families celebrate [[@ganesh-chaturthi|Ganesh Chaturthi]] and Diwali with their own sweets and dishes. Many Goan Hindu dishes skip vinegar and use kokum and coconut instead, but the coast's love of fish, rice and [[@coconut|coconut]] runs through every Goan kitchen.
